content: To prevent cervical cancer, precancerous lesions should be managed through a systematic approach. Screening begins with cytology (commonly known as a Pap smear), followed by colposcopy. Colposcopy may or may not include a biopsy, depending on the findings. If treatment is required, cryotherapy is the preferred method. However, if cryotherapy is not suitable, Loop Electrosurgical Excision Procedure (LEEP) should be performed. For women with a positive colposcopic impression, a biopsy can be performed to confirm the diagnosis histologically, or treatment can be initiated immediately without a biopsy. If the colposcopy results are normal, rescreening should be conducted within three years. If a woman is eligible for cryotherapy, the lesion should be treated with cryotherapy. If she is not eligible for cryotherapy, LEEP should be used instead. Post-treatment follow-up is recommended one year after the procedure to ensure the effectiveness of the treatment and monitor for recurrence. For women with atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance (ASCUS) or more severe cytological abnormalities, colposcopy is indicated. If the colposcopy findings are positive, treatment or further evaluation should follow. If the colposcopy findings are negative, rescreening should occur within three years. If the findings are suspicious for cancer, the patient should be referred for appropriate diagnostic and therapeutic interventions. If a biopsy is performed and confirms cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or higher (CIN2+), treatment with cryotherapy or LEEP is recommended. If the biopsy reveals CIN1 or less, rescreening should be conducted within three years. For women with HIV-positive status or unknown HIV status in areas with high endemic rates of HIV infection, cytology screening is particularly important. The management of these cases should follow the same principles, with adjustments based on the patient’s immune status and local guidelines. The World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines provide detailed recommendations for screening and treating precancerous cervical lesions. These guidelines also include considerations for selecting appropriate strategies based on individual patient factors and resource availability. For further guidance, refer to Chapter 3 of the WHO guidelines. In terms of diagnostic test accuracy, various methods such as HPV testing, visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA), Pap testing (cytology), and colposcopy have been evaluated. Studies have compared these methods to determine their effectiveness in detecting cervical neoplasia. HPV testing has shown high sensitivity for detecting high-grade lesions, while VIA and Pap testing remain valuable tools, particularly in resource-limited settings. Colposcopy, often used as a diagnostic tool, has variable accuracy depending on the setting and the expertise of the practitioner. The WHO guidelines also include systematic reviews and meta-analyses of studies evaluating the performance of these diagnostic methods. These reviews highlight the importance of using evidence-based approaches to optimize cervical cancer prevention strategies.
